pedagogy.summary: At 7-9 this is a CLASSIFICATION topic: extend the child's mental map of the solar system beyond the eight planets to the smaller bodies, and pin down three commonly-confused categories. Asteroids = rocky bodies, mostly in the belt between Mars and Jupiter. Comets = icy 'dirty snowballs' that grow a glowing tail only when they near the Sun (ice vaporises). And the meteoroid→meteor→meteorite trio, which is ONE object named by WHERE it is: a rock in space (meteoroid), a streak of light as it burns through our atmosphere (meteor / 'shooting star'), and what's left if it lands (meteorite). The load-bearing moves are (1) rocky-vs-icy for asteroid-vs-comet, and (2) location-defines-the-name for the meteor trio.
bestPractices: Teach by contrasting pairs with a clear discriminator: asteroid = ROCK, comet = ICE (+dust). Anchor comets as 'dirty snowballs' and asteroids as 'space rocks in the belt between Mars and Jupiter'.

Make the meteor trio a JOURNEY, not three separate things: same object, three names by location — meteoroid (in space) → meteor (burning streak in the atmosphere) → meteorite (landed on the ground). A single labelled arc from space to ground fixes it.

Surface the counter-intuitive comet-tail fact explicitly: a comet's tail is pushed out by sunlight and the solar wind, so it always points AWAY from the Sun — it does not trail behind the comet like a scarf. This is memorable and corrects a strong intuition.
Correct 'shooting star' language directly — a meteor is a burning space rock, not a star — tying back to the child's earlier learning that stars are Suns.
Place the new objects on the solar-system map they already know (from The Eight Planets): the belt sits between Mars and Jupiter; comets swing in from far away and loop around the Sun.
keyRepresentations: Solar-system map with the asteroid belt drawn as a ring of rubble between Mars and Jupiter
Side-by-side 'rocky asteroid vs icy comet' comparison card
Comet diagram: icy nucleus + coma + tail, with the tail pointing away from the Sun along the orbit
A single labelled journey arc: meteoroid (space) → meteor (streak in atmosphere) → meteorite (on the ground)
Size/where-they-live sorting mat (belt / near the Sun with a tail / entering our sky)
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a comet's tail streams out BEHIND it like exhaust or a scarf, rather than always pointing away from the Sun.
Believing comets are burning / on fire — they are icy; the tail is vaporising ice and dust lit by sunlight, not flames.
Using meteoroid, meteor and meteorite interchangeably, not realising they are the same object named by location (space / atmosphere / ground).
Calling a meteor a 'shooting star' and thinking it really is a star.
Assuming asteroids are scattered everywhere or are tiny planets, rather than mostly rocky bodies concentrated in the belt.
Confusing asteroids and comets — not grasping rocky-vs-icy as the key difference.

learn.summary: A classification topic for ages 7-9: extend the child's map of the solar system beyond the eight planets to smaller bodies and pin down three commonly-confused categories. Asteroids are rocky bodies mostly in the belt between Mars and Jupiter; comets are icy 'dirty snowballs' that grow a glowing tail only when near the Sun (ice vaporises); and meteoroid→meteor→meteorite is ONE rock named by WHERE it is (a rock in space, the glowing streak of light as it burns in the atmosphere, and the landed rock). The two load-bearing moves are rocky-vs-icy (asteroid vs comet) and location-defines-the-name (meteor trio). A counter-intuitive fact to surface: a comet's tail is pushed by sunlight and the solar wind, so it always points AWAY from the Sun, not trailing behind the comet's motion.

activities.title: Explore the solar-system map: tap and reveal the small bodies
feedback: If the child merges the categories, sort them aloud: rocky asteroids (belt between Mars and Jupiter), icy comets (tails near the Sun), and the meteoroid→meteor→meteorite journey of one small rock.
When the child ties the tail to the comet's direction of travel, point to the flap: the tail points away from the Sun whichever way the comet moves.

If the child calls the streak a star, name the three stages and explain the streak is light from a tiny space rock burning up in our air, not a star, tying back to earlier learning that stars are Suns.
activities.rationale: The core objective is to identify and classify fixed categories, so a tappable illustration can present these distinctions and place the new objects on the familiar planet map to anchor them, giving at-a-glance coverage. A static scene can assert the tail rule but cannot let the child manipulate it, so pair it with the orbit activity.
sourceClaims: Comets are icy bodies ('made of ice and dust—not rock', unlike rocky asteroids) that grow a tail as they near the Sun because the ice vaporises; the ion tail always points directly away from the Sun. Most asteroids lie in the belt between Mars and Jupiter.

A meteoroid is a space rock in space; if it enters Earth's atmosphere it vaporises into a meteor (a streak of light, sometimes called a 'shooting star', but not actually a star); if it survives and lands it is a meteorite.
learnerActions: Start from a single wide solar-system scene the child already recognises: Sun, inner planets, and the asteroid belt drawn as a ring of rubble between Mars and Jupiter, plus a comet on a looping path and a meteor streaking into Earth's sky.
Tap the rubble-ring between Mars and Jupiter so it lights up and is labelled: 'asteroids — space rocks, mostly in the belt between Mars and Jupiter.'
Tap the bright comet and zoom into its icy nucleus, fuzzy coma, and streaming tail; read that a comet is an icy 'dirty snowball' that grows a tail only when it nears the Sun.
Lift a flap asking 'which way does the tail point?' and discover it points AWAY from the Sun, not behind the comet like a scarf or exhaust.

Tap the 'shooting star' streak and follow one glowing arc that splits into three labelled stages: meteoroid (a rock in space) → meteor (the glowing streak of light made as the rock burns in the sky) → meteorite (any piece of the rock that survives and lands on the ground; most burn up completely).

Lift a final flap on the 'shooting star' to reveal it is not a star at all: the bright streak is the light made when a tiny space rock burns up in our air — the rock itself is the meteoroid, and the glowing streak is the meteor.
activities.intendedInsight: Asteroids are rocky and live in the belt; comets are icy and grow a tail (which points away from the Sun) only near the Sun; and meteoroid/meteor/meteorite name the SAME rock by where it is — a rock in space (meteoroid), the streak of light it makes while burning up (meteor), and the landed rock (meteorite), so a 'shooting star' is a light-streak, not a star.

activities.title: Drag the comet round its orbit and watch the tail swing
feedback: If the child expects the tail to trail behind the motion, trace the comet round the Sun so they see the tail swing to lead the comet on the way out.
Name the cause explicitly: sunlight and the solar wind blow the gas and dust away from the Sun.
Reinforce that the tail is vaporising ice and dust lit by sunlight, not flames — a comet is icy, not on fire.
activities.rationale: The tail-direction idea is dynamic and counter-intuitive, so letting the child move the comet and see the tail re-orient can make the 'points away from the Sun' rule concrete in a way a fixed picture only states. This is offered as a helpful dynamic scaffold, not as the only way to grasp the idea.
sourceClaims: Comets are icy bodies ('made of ice and dust—not rock', unlike rocky asteroids) that grow a tail as they near the Sun because the ice vaporises; the ion tail always points directly away from the Sun. Most asteroids lie in the belt between Mars and Jupiter.
learnerActions: Drag a comet along an elliptical orbit around the Sun.
As the comet approaches the Sun, watch the tail lengthen and bloom; as it moves away again, watch it shrink.

Pay attention to the tail's direction as the comet rounds the Sun: watch it continuously re-orient to point away from the Sun, so that on the outbound leg the tail actually LEADS the comet rather than trailing it.
Predict, before dragging, which way the tail will point when the comet is heading back out, then check.
activities.intendedInsight: A comet's tail is pushed away from the Sun by sunlight and the solar wind, so it always points away from the Sun regardless of which way the comet is travelling — and it grows only when the comet is near enough for its ices to warm and stream off.

activities.title: Sort and sequence the small bodies
feedback: If sorting fails, re-anchor the discriminators: asteroid = ROCK in the belt, comet = ICE with a tail that points away from the Sun, meteor trio = one rock named by where it is.
If the child sequences the trio wrongly, walk the single arc from space to ground and re-label each stage.
If the child says the tail trails behind, revisit the orbit activity: the Sun, not the motion, sets the tail's direction.
activities.rationale: Categorisation, matching and sequencing map neatly onto this content and are well suited to checking the classifications and vocabulary after teaching. This checks and consolidates learning rather than building the initial mental map, so use it after the exploration and tail activities; sorting and matching alone do not by themselves show independent explanation, so include the 'explain why' prompt.
sourceClaims: A meteoroid is a space rock in space; if it enters Earth's atmosphere it vaporises into a meteor (a streak of light, sometimes called a 'shooting star', but not actually a star); if it survives and lands it is a meteorite.
learnerActions: Sort a set of objects into three bins: rocky asteroid (belt), icy comet (tail near the Sun), and meteor-journey.
Put the meteoroid→meteor→meteorite stages in order and label each by its location (space / atmosphere / ground).
Answer: which way does a comet's tail point, and where in the solar system do most asteroids orbit?
Explain in your own words why a comet grows a tail only when it comes close to the Sun.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure recall and discrimination of the three categories and the naming-by-location rule for the meteor trio, including the surprising tail direction.

constraints: Keep the two load-bearing discriminators explicit: rocky-vs-icy (asteroid vs comet) and location-defines-the-name (meteor trio).

A static tap-reveal scene can present the categories and assert the tail rule, but cannot let the child manipulate the comet; the orbit drag activity is what lets the child act on and check the 'tail points away from the Sun' behaviour.

The sort/sequence activity checks and consolidates classifications rather than building the initial mental map; treat it as consolidation or assessment after teaching, since sorting-and-matching responses do not by themselves show independent explanation.

A 3D fly-through alongside a comet or through the belt can convey scale and scatter and makes an atmospheric set-piece, but the concept is categorical not spatial, so keep it optional and not the core teach.

An in-role dialogue can rehearse or recite the category names, but does not itself provide the at-a-glance sorting or the visual tail-direction reveal; if used, pair it with the visual map rather than relying on it alone.

Name the meteor trio precisely: the meteoroid is the rock in space, the meteor is the glowing streak of light it makes while burning in the atmosphere, and the meteorite is the rock once it has landed.
Correct 'shooting star' language directly: the streak is light made when a tiny space rock burns up in our air, not a star, tying back to the child's earlier learning that stars are Suns.
Present a comet as icy, not burning: the tail is vaporising ice and dust lit by sunlight, not flames.
Keep the comet-tail rule at the age-appropriate 'always points away from the Sun'; the ion-vs-dust-tail nuance is not needed in learner text but should not be contradicted.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy entry included claims framed as universal (e.g. 3D 'adds spectacle without being needed', a static picture 'can only assert', a conversation 'cannot deliver' the sorting). These comparative-necessity claims are not established by the available sources and have been softened to scoped affordances/limits in constraints.

The outbound-leg detail — that the tail LEADS the comet when it heads away from the Sun — follows from the sourced 'tail always points away from the Sun' claim and is physically correct; it is retained as a stretch point for able learners but may be advanced for some 7-9 children.

The simplified 'single tail always points away from the Sun' is an approximation of the sourced 'ion tail' claim: the ion/gas tail points directly away, while a comet's dust tail curves and partly lags. The simplification is appropriate for ages 7-9 and is used in learner text, with the nuance recorded here only.
The meteor trio is named precisely so the meteor is the light-streak and the meteoroid the rock; this avoids conflating the object with the phenomenon in learner-facing text.
Source claims cite the teaching facts (NASA Space Place) and support the stated principles; they do not constitute evidence that these specific activities were tested for effectiveness.

probeDeeper: Where in the solar system do most asteroids orbit?
What is the SAME small rock called when it's out in space, streaking through our air, and lying on the ground?
Why does a comet only grow a tail when it comes close to the Sun?
If a comet is now heading back OUT, away from the Sun, which way does its tail point?
assess.correctAnswer: The tail does NOT simply trail behind the comet's motion. A comet's tail always points AWAY FROM THE SUN, whichever way the comet happens to be travelling, because sunlight and the solar wind push the comet's gas and dust away from the Sun. So as a comet rounds the Sun and heads back out, its tail actually goes ahead of it — still pointing away from the Sun. (A comet is an icy body that only grows a tail when it nears the Sun and its ices warm and stream off.)

errorPatterns.pattern: a comet's tail trails out behind it, like smoke behind a rocket ('it follows the direction it's moving')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that sunlight and the solar wind blow the tail away from the Sun; trace a comet round the Sun so the child sees the tail swing to LEAD the comet on the way out.
errorPatterns.distractor: The tail always streams out behind the comet, in the direction it came from.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child ties the tail direction to the comet's motion rather than to the Sun

errorPatterns.pattern: asteroids, comets and meteors are all just the same kind of thing
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort them: rocky asteroids (mostly the belt between Mars and Jupiter), icy comets (tails near the Sun), and the meteoroid→meteor→meteorite journey of one small rock.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child uses the words interchangeably and cannot sort them

errorPatterns.pattern: a shooting star is a real star falling out of the sky
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explain it's a tiny space rock burning up in our atmosphere, not a star; name it meteoroid in space, meteor as the streak, meteorite if it lands.
errorPatterns.distractor: A shooting star is a real star falling out of the sky.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child calls the meteor streak a star

responseLevels.gap: Merges asteroids/comets/meteors and pictures the tail trailing behind the comet's motion.
responseLevels.full: Explains the tail points away from the Sun (pushed by sunlight and solar wind), distinguishes asteroid from comet, and names the meteoroid→meteor→meteorite journey of one rock.
responseLevels.partial: Distinguishes rocky asteroids from icy comets and knows the meteor trio, but still has the tail trailing behind, or is unsure which way it points.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A comet is racing through space and grows a long glowing tail. Does the tail always trail out BEHIND the comet, in the direction it came from — like smoke behind a rocket? Or does it point some other way? Tell me WHY.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The intuitive 'tail trails behind like exhaust' picture is what almost every child brings. Only a child who knows the Sun pushes the tail says it points away from the Sun regardless of motion — and can handle the surprising outbound case where the tail leads. The 'why' tier exposes whether they think motion or the Sun sets the tail's direction.
